The best placed to comment on how Bitcoin mining affects electricity prices is the grid operator. So what did the operator of the grid with the most Bitcoin mining say about its effect on price?

Brad Jones, former interim CEO of Texas’ grid ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas), stated plainly that Bitcoin mining “**[[0|helped keep the price of power low]]** for all Texans”. Jones then described several ways that Bitcoin mining helped keep prices low.

1. Making use of wind and solar energy that would otherwise have been wasted. As Jones put it, Bitcoin mining helped “find a home for otherwise wasted wind energy.” Because of that, those wind and solar farms made more money and could expand. That meant more supply of power, which naturally eases pressure on prices.

2. By creating a more competitive market for demand response. Here, energy users compete in a Dutch auction to provide a key service to the grid. The service is switching off their power use instantly when demand peaks, when generation goes offline, or both. Steel works and aluminum smelters used to supply demand response. But they could shed only part of their load, and smelters for only around [[1|four hours]] before their pots began to freeze. Bitcoin mining could shed its entire load within [[2|500 milliseconds]]. It could also keep providing the service [[3|for days]]. With another competitor in the market, [[4|grid operators paid less]] for demand response, which lowered power prices for consumers.

3. As the share of [[5|solar and wind]] on a grid grows, grid operators usually have to buy more gas peaker plants. These are gas plants that run only when demand peaks. They supply backup power for when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining at the same time.

Not only do these plants sit [[6|idle]] most of the year and release CO2 whenever they fire up, but they are [[7|very expensive]]. In Texas, Brad Jones used a more practical solution: he arranged for Bitcoin mining companies to power down. That meant the new gas peaker plants proposed by Hathaway Energy didn’t need to fire up. In fact, Texas did not need to buy these gas peaker plants at all. According to the Digital Assets Research Institute, that [[8|saved the grid operator $18 billion]]. This saving further reduced the need for ERCOT to raise power prices.

[[9|After inflation]], home electricity prices in Texas have stayed essentially flat since Bitcoin mining came onto the ERCOT grid. The average was 15.4 cents/kWh before June 2021 and 15.9 cents since, in 2026 dollars. Yet over the same period, [[10|the price of natural gas for homes]], which fuels much of Texas’s power, rose by about 23% after inflation. This backs up Brad Jones’ observation that Bitcoin mining in fact “Helped keep the price of power low for all Texans.”

4. In places such as the UK, the grid operator often has to pay a wind or solar farm if it cannot take its power [[11|(called curtailment)]]. These fees can be very high, so the operator has to charge higher prices to stay profitable. For example, the UK recently spent £2.5 million on a single day of curtailment (see image below). It would not have had to pay this if Bitcoin mines had been [[12|located at the wind farm]].
When Bitcoin mining companies use that otherwise curtailed (wasted) energy, the grid operator no longer has to pay these large fees.

In Texas (ERCOT), 2020 data showed 4.87 million MWh (megawatt-hours, a unit of electricity) curtailed, mostly wind. **[[13|Niaz et al]]** found that mining farms could use up to 93% of it in their lowest-cost scenarios. That would turn waste into $239 million in profits for the grid operator. The authors also found that Bitcoin mining **reduces curtailment risks in PPAs** (power purchase agreements).

5. Grid upgrades are very expensive. The cost is passed on either to taxpayers or directly to power users. A recent Duke University study showed that Bitcoin mining could help the grid operator delay, or in some cases [[14|avoid, costly grid upgrades]].
As well as Texas, other parts of the world have found out firsthand how power prices can suddenly and violently spike when Bitcoin mining companies leave the grid.

In Sept 2024, for example, residents of Hadsel in northern Norway realized that Bitcoin mining had for years been keeping their power bills about [[15|20% lower]]. When the Bitcoin mine [[16|left the grid]], their local grid company Noranett lost about 20% of its revenue. It raised household bills by more than 20% to cover the [[17|shortfall]].

Meanwhile, [[18|CNBC reported]] that adding Bitcoin mining to a rural microgrid in Kenya “dropped the price of power from 35 cents per kilowatt hour to 25 cents per kWh”. That was a 28.5% price cut for rural power users. Bitcoin mining did this by using hydro energy that was previously wasted.
